definition: Optimization involving objective functions with multiple local minima, saddle points, or other complexities, lacking the strong theoretical guarantees of convex optimization.
details: Deep neural network training is a canonical example of non-convex optimization, yet empirically, techniques like SGD and its variants have proven remarkably effective at finding good solutions despite the lack of theoretical convergence guarantees.

explainer.lead: Non-convex optimization covers objectives with multiple local minima, saddle points, and other structure that rules out convex guarantees. It matters because training deep neural networks is exactly this kind of problem, yet practical methods find good solutions.

tiers.eli5: It is like finding the lowest point in a mountain range full of valleys, where no method promises the very lowest, but walking downhill usually gets somewhere good.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers rely on SGD and its variants, tuning learning rates and schedules, because convergence guarantees do not apply and empirical behaviour is the guide. Pitfall: treating a low training loss as proof of a global optimum ignores that the landscape may have many good and bad basins.
tiers.paperLevel: Formally, minimize f(x) where f has multiple local minima or saddle points; unlike convex problems, no general polynomial-time guarantee of global optimality holds. Known limits: theory gives conditions for convergence to stationary points, not to the global minimum.

explainer.example: Training a deep network with SGD can end in different local solutions with different validation accuracy depending on initialization and learning-rate schedule.
